decisions.name: HandMaintainedVersionString
decisions.what: appVersion is a hand-edited Text constant rather than read from cabal-generated Paths_pelotero_engine.version
why: Reading from Paths_* requires plumbing the autogen module into the import graph and pulls Data.Version handling into every site that logs the version.
The risk is drift: bumping the .cabal version without bumping this constant produces a binary that lies about itself in the fetch log.
Mitigation is process: a release checklist item, not a code-level guarantee.

appName: compile-time constant; canonical application name used in logging and any place that needs to identify this binary as the producer of a record
OverloadedStrings is enabled solely so the string literal types as Text without explicit pack
appVersion: hand-maintained version string; not derived from cabal's PackageInfo_pelotero_engine, so it can drift from the .cabal file unless updated by hand
intended to be embedded wherever the engine identifies itself (audit fields, fetch-log enrichment)

decisions.name: SingleHelperEliminatesImplicitContract
decisions.what: All upstream-id <-> external_id Text encodings live in this one module; every site that crosses that boundary calls a typed helper rather than rolling its own T.pack . show
why: The legacy pattern (T.pack . show . unTeamId scattered across Sync.Players, Sync.Schedule, Sync.Boxscores) was an implicit string contract; if anyone changed one site without changing the others, every game upsert silently skipped because resolveTeam returned Nothing for every team.
Centralising the encoding makes the contract a function call: changing the encoding requires editing one module, and the type system enforces that callers go through the helper.
The roundtrip property (externalIdToTeamId . externalIdFromTeamId === Just) is checked by Hedgehog so encoding drift between forward and reverse paths is caught at test time.

decisions.name: PerIdTypePairsNotPolymorphic
decisions.what: Six concrete functions (one from + one to per id type) rather than a single class-based polymorphic encoder
why: Three id types is below the threshold where typeclass machinery earns its keep; six monomorphic helpers are easier to grep, easier to test, and easier to read at call sites.
If a fourth id type appears (e.g. ProviderInternal player ids using a different scheme), this is the place to revisit; until then, monomorphic wins.

externalIdFromTeamId: TeamId -> Text via T.pack . show . unTeamId
stable byte-for-byte: this is the canonical wire encoding stored in team_external_id.external_id
externalIdFromPlayerId: PlayerId -> Text via T.pack . show . unPlayerId
consumed by Sync.Players.upsertAllPlayers and Sync.Boxscores.upsertEntries (forward) and Sync.Boxscores.syncOne (reverse via the roundtrip)
externalIdFromGameId: GameId -> Text via T.pack . show . unGameId
externalIdToTeamId: Text -> Maybe TeamId; reads via Text.Read.readMaybe and wraps in TeamId
returns Nothing on any non-integer or negative value; an empty Text returns Nothing

decisions.name: KatipPatternLiftedFromCheeblr
decisions.what: Logging effect uses the Katip pattern: logFM, logItem, addNamespace, addContext; production interpreter writes structured JSON to stdout
why: Cheeblr already runs this pattern in production with structured search-friendly JSON logs; reusing it means we get the same querying, the same tooling, and one less invented wheel.
Structured logs make per-warning grepping (e.g. 'all UnknownPosition warnings in the last week') a one-line jq query rather than a regex over freeform text.

Stdout-only at the application layer; the runtime (systemd / OCI runtime / k8s) handles persistence and rotation. We deliberately avoid in-process file rotation because it duplicates the runtime's job.

decisions.name: ReplacesConvertLogWarnings
decisions.what: Pelotero.MLB.Convert.logWarnings (direct stderr IO) is gone; warning emission goes through Logging.logFM with structured fields
why: Convert.logWarnings wrote bare stderr lines with a 'convert: ' prefix; the prefix was the only structure log scrapers had to grab onto.
Going through Logging means each ConvertWarning becomes a structured log item with its constructor name as a tag; downstream systems can filter on the tag, not on string-prefix scraping.
The Handle-parameterised logWarningsTo indirection existed only to make logWarnings testable; with a capturing test interpreter (runLoggingCapture), that indirection disappears.

logFM: Logging send-only; structured log emission with severity + message
production: writes a JSON line to stdout via Katip's stdout scribe
test: appends to an IORef-backed [LogLine] under runLoggingCapture, or no-ops under runLoggingDiscard
logItem: Logging send-only; logs a Katip-LogItem-encodable payload with a severity
used for richer structured events (e.g. SyncResult summaries) where a plain text message loses the structure
addNamespace: Logging operation; runs an inner Eff under a nested Katip namespace
used to scope all logs from a syncRosters call under e.g. 'sync.rosters' so traces are easy to filter
addContext: Logging operation; attaches structured key/value context to all logs emitted by the inner Eff
carries through to JSON output as additional fields on each log line

runLoggingKatip.intent: Production interpreter; writes JSON-formatted log lines to stdout via Katip's stdout scribe
notes: scribes and namespace are wired once at startup
stdout-only; the runtime is responsible for persistence/rotation

runLoggingCapture.intent: Test interpreter that captures every emitted log into an IORef-backed [LogLine] returned alongside the inner action's result
notes: uses IOE because it needs an IORef; not pure
captures the structured payload (severity, namespace, message), suitable for asserting 'these warnings were emitted in this order' in property tests

runLoggingDiscard.intent: Test interpreter that silently drops every log; pure (no effects on the inner stack)
notes: default for tests that don't care about logging output
leaves the rest of the effect stack untouched so callers don't have to thread IOE just to silence logs

decisions.name: PureKernelSplitFromEffects
decisions.what: scorePlayerPure / sumBattingPoints / sumPitchingPoints / rowToBattingStats / rowToPitchingStats are pure and exported separately from the effectful scoreLeague / scoreTeam
why: The pure kernel is the part hedgehog tests can hit without spinning up Postgres.
Splitting them lets us unit-test 'given these rows, the score is X' without an in-memory effect runner — just a record literal and a function call.

The pure functions deliberately take and return DB row types (BattingRow / PitchingRow), not domain types, because the round-trip BattingRow -> BattingStats -> Points loses no information; storing-then-loading and direct-scoring agree by construction.

decisions.name: MissingLeagueReturnsNothing
decisions.what: scoreLeague and scoreTeam both return Maybe; Nothing means the league config (or the team) wasn't in the DB
why: Distinguishes 'this league doesn't exist' from 'this league has zero teams' (Just LeagueScore { lscTeams = [] }).
An empty lineup still produces a TeamScore with zero points — dropping such teams would be a presentation choice the caller should make.
Doesn't validate that the team belongs to the league in scoreTeam — caller's responsibility to check.

decisions.name: PitOutsIsCanonicalNoTextRoundTrip
decisions.what: rowToPitchingStats passes pitOuts straight through from the DB row; pitInningsPitched no longer exists in PitchingStats
why: Phase B.1 collapsed the redundant pitInningsPitched (Maybe Text) + pitOuts (Maybe Int) pair into pitOuts only. The wire-format string is parsed at convert time and discarded; the DB stores outs; readers see outs.

Removes the parseInningsPitched . renderInningsPitched round-trip that previously lived in the score path. Saves one parse and one render per pitching row, more importantly removes a class of subtle bug (a future caller setting pitOuts only would have been silently zeroed by the round-trip).
scorePitching now reads pitOuts directly without any parse step.

decisions.name: PeriodFromUtcStartEnd
decisions.what: scoreLeague derives lscPeriodStart / lscPeriodEnd by utctDay'ing lcScoringStart and lcScoringEnd from the league config
why: league_config stores UTCTime instants because lineup-lock cutoffs are timezone-sensitive (see Pelotero.Domain.League decision ScoringPeriodAsUtcTime), but the DB game.game_date is Day, so the query needs Day bounds.
Truncating UTCTime to Day in UTC is correct only because game_date is also stored in UTC at write time. A change to either column's timezone semantics would break this silently.
The two utctDay calls happen once per scoreLeague invocation; not a perf concern.

decisions.name: PerGamePlayerMapBuilds
decisions.what: buildPlayerMaps issues one BoxscoreEntry.getBattingForGame and one BoxscoreEntry.getPitchingForGame per game id and bucks the results into Map DbPlayerId [Row] in Haskell
why: BoxscoreEntry only exposes per-game queries today. A single date-range query would be the right shape (and is the planned C.2 work), but adding it requires extending both the DB module and the effect.
Per-game queries keep the Score module honest about its dependencies — it asks for what BoxscoreEntry actually offers — at the cost of N round-trips per scoring period.
Acceptable for current league sizes (a 30-day period is ~450 games for one MLB league) but explicitly a known performance gap; C.2 is the optimisation.

decisions.name: ScoringReadsFromLineupSnapshots
decisions.what: scoreOneTeam reads from LineupSnapshot.getSnapshotForTeamGame keyed by (league_team_id, game_id), NOT from the team's current lineup_slot rows
why: Phase B.3 fixed the correctness bug where scoring used the current lineup against historical games. Real fantasy leagues lock lineups daily; mid-period lineup edits used to retroactively change prior days' scores.
The scoring loop is now per-game (which it should always have been): for each game in the period, read the snapshot for that team for that game, score that game's stats against that snapshot, sum.
Re-running scoring at any point gives the same answer for the same (league, period, team) triple. This is the invariant owners were checking against and losing trust over.

rowToBattingStats: mechanical Int32 -> Int widening on every Maybe field; lossless
rowToPitchingStats: Int32 -> Int widening on every Maybe field; lossless
pitOuts is preserved straight from the row; no Text reconstruction (post Phase B.1)
sumBattingPoints: sumPoints over (scoreBatting m . rowToBattingStats) — a fold; empty list yields zeroPoints
scorePlayerPure: produces a PlayerScore with batting + pitching subtotals and their sum
pure: same inputs -> same output, no IO or randomness
the canonical hedgehog target for scoring property tests

scoreLeague.intent: Score every team in a league across the league's configured scoring period using snapshotted lineups
notes: returns Nothing if the league config row is absent
empty lineups produce zero-point TeamScores rather than being dropped
uses LineupSnapshot.getSnapshotForTeamGame, NOT LineupSlot.getSlotsForTeam — see decision ScoringReadsFromLineupSnapshots
deterministic across re-runs: same (league, period) inputs always yield the same scores

scoreTeam: scores a single team using the league's period
returns Nothing if either the league config or the team is absent
does NOT validate that the team belongs to the league
buildPlayerMaps: takes [DbGameId] (the games in the period); the caller (collectGameIds) gets these from Games.getGamesByDateRange
issues one Box.getBattingForGame and one Box.getPitchingForGame per game id; bucks results into Map DbPlayerId [BattingRow] and Map DbPlayerId [PitchingRow] via Map.fromListWith (++)
exactly N+N database round trips for an N-game period; collapsing this into a single date-range query is planned C.2 work
scoreOneTeam: per-game inner loop: for each game id, fetch the team's lineup snapshot for that game via LineupSnapshot.getSnapshotForTeamGame, score that game's stats, then aggregate per-player scores across games via Map.fromListWith mergePlayerScores
internal helper; not exported; signature subject to change
scoreTeamForGame: internal; for a (team, game) pair: read the snapshot rows, look up each player's batting/pitching for that specific game, score with scorePlayerPure
filter step inside scoreOnePlayerForGame discards rows from other games in the period maps
scoreOnePlayerForGame: internal; given a player and a game id, filter the player's period rows to only that game's, then call scorePlayerPure
a player on the snapshot with no boxscore activity for that game gets zero points (filter yields empty lists)
mergePlayerScores: internal; pointwise addition of two PlayerScores, used when aggregating per-game scores for the same player across multiple games
collectGameIds: internal helper; calls Games.getGamesByDateRange and mapMaybes the gameRowId field

decisions.name: SnapshotPerGamePerTeamWithExistsCheck
decisions.what: snapshotLineupsForGame copies the current lineup_slot rows into lineup_snapshot keyed by (league_team_id, game_id); idempotency is enforced both by an explicit 'snapshot exists?' check at the orchestration level and by a UNIQUE constraint at the table level
why: The (league_team_id, game_id) key gives us 'what was this team's lineup for this specific game'. Re-running scoring against a snapshot gives a deterministic answer.

Once a snapshot exists for a (team, game) pair, it is treated as locked-in and is NOT overwritten by re-running. ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING in writeSnapshotsT plus the explicit pre-check together ensure 'first snapshot wins'. This deliberately prevents late-edit scenarios where an owner changes a lineup after the snapshot job ran.
There is no game-start-time guard at the orchestration level; the schema only tracks game_date (Day), not a precise instant. Operators are responsible for scheduling snapshots before first pitch.

decisions.name: TypedResultNotUnit
decisions.what: snapshotLineupsForTeam returns PerTeamResult and snapshotLineupsForGame returns SnapshotResult; both are aggregates that surface counts (teams snapshotted vs already-done, rows inserted)
why: An earlier sketch had snapshotLineupsForGame return (); operators couldn't tell whether anything happened.

PerTeamResult has two constructors: TeamSnapshotted Int (n rows submitted to the snapshot table for this team — the number reflects rows attempted; under concurrent snapshot jobs ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING could silently drop duplicates so n may overstate actual inserts in that case) and TeamAlreadyHasSnapshot (snapshotExistsForTeamGame returned True; nothing was written).

SnapshotResult is a record { snapTeamsSnapshotted, snapTeamsAlreadyDone, snapRowsInserted } with a Monoid instance: mempty is all zeros and (<>) is pointwise addition, so the per-league aggregation is just mconcat.

decisions.name: ModuleLivesInLineupNotEffects
decisions.what: snapshot orchestration lives at Pelotero.Lineup.Snapshot, not under Pelotero.Effects
why: This module composes multiple effects (LineupSlot, LineupSnapshot, LeagueConfig, LeagueTeam, Logging) to do a piece of business logic; it is not itself an effect definition.
Pelotero.Effects.LineupSnapshot is the dispatch interface; Pelotero.Lineup.Snapshot is the orchestration layer that uses it.
Mirrors the layering between Pelotero.Sync.* (orchestration) and Pelotero.Effects.* (dispatch).

decisions.name: EmptyLineupCornerCase
decisions.what: If a team has no lineup_slot rows at snapshot time, snapshotLineupsForTeam writes zero rows and returns TeamSnapshotted 0; the snapshotExistsForTeamGame query will subsequently return False (no rows), so a re-run with a non-empty lineup will write a fresh snapshot
why: This is a deliberate quirk: empty-lineup snapshots and 'no snapshot taken' are indistinguishable at the storage level.

In practice this is desirable — a team that joins late and has no lineup at the first snapshot should still get scored once they set one — but it does mean 'TeamSnapshotted 0' is operationally meaningful.

snapshotLineupsForTeam.intent: Snapshot one team's current lineup for one game; idempotent on (team, game)
notes: first calls LSnap.snapshotExistsForTeamGame; if True, returns TeamAlreadyHasSnapshot without touching lineup_slot
if False, reads the team's lineup via LS.getSlotsForTeam, projects each slot row to a LineupSnapshotRow tagged with the game id, and writes via LSnap.writeSnapshots
logs an InfoS event with team/game/row count on the success path

snapshotLineupsForGame.intent: Snapshot every team in every active league for one game
notes: loads all LeagueConfig rows via LC.getAll, filters to those with lcStatus == "active"
for each active league, fetches league teams via LT.getForLeague and snapshots each via snapshotLineupsForTeam
aggregates per-team results into a SnapshotResult and logs an InfoS summary

toSnapshot: internal helper; projects (DbGameId, LineupSlotRow) into a LineupSnapshotRow

decisions.name: TeamsBeforePlayersOrdering
decisions.what: syncRosters upserts all teams first, builds a TeamId -> DbTeamId map, then upserts players using that map to resolve playerRowCurrentTeamId
why: Players carry a foreign key to team via current_team_id; if the team doesn't exist in the DB at insert time, the FK either fails (with constraint enforcement) or installs a dangling reference (without).
Building the map in memory between the two phases avoids a second round-trip per player to look up the DB team id.
The two phases share one syncedAt timestamp from the Clock effect, so last_synced_at on team and player rows match exactly for a given sync run, useful when reasoning about staleness.

decisions.name: ProviderAgnosticEntryPoint
decisions.what: syncRosters takes already-converted [Team] and [Player] domain values plus a precomputed SHA-256, never touches wire types or HTTP
why: Keeps the sync pipeline testable in isolation: tests construct domain values directly and run against in-memory effect interpreters.
Allows alternative providers (a future non-MLB feed, manual data import) to reuse this exact code path by doing their own wire->domain conversion upstream.
The SHA is computed by the caller because only the caller has the raw bytes; passing it in here keeps this module from depending on Crypto.Hash.

decisions.name: ResourceLiteralActiveRosters
decisions.what: syncRosters writes fetchLogResource = 'active-rosters' as a literal rather than parameterising it
why: The MLB roster endpoint queried (rosterUrl) filters to activeStatus=ACTIVE on the server side, so this resource name is the literal truth of what was fetched.
If a future scope adds inactive/40-man/minor-league fetches, that becomes a new resource name passed in by the caller, not a flag here.

decisions.name: ExternalIdViaCentralisedHelper
decisions.what: upsertAllTeams and upsertAllPlayers call Pelotero.Provider.ExternalId.externalIdFromTeamId / externalIdFromPlayerId, never inline T.pack . show
why: Phase A.1 collapsed the implicit cross-module string contract into a typed helper. The sync pipeline now goes through one canonical encoding for all upstream id -> Text conversions.
The Hedgehog roundtrip property (externalIdToTeamId . externalIdFromTeamId === Just) catches any future encoding drift at test time.
Sync.Schedule.resolveTeam uses the matching reverse function (externalIdToTeamId via the lookup); both sides go through the same module.

decisions.name: TotalHandCharFromDomain
decisions.what: upsertAllPlayers uses Pelotero.Domain.Player.handChar (total) instead of T.head . renderHandedness (partial)
why: Phase A.6 introduced handChar :: Handedness -> Char as an exhaustive case-of in the domain layer. T.head's partiality is gone because the conversion is no longer a Text indexing operation.

The total function lives next to the Handedness type so any new constructor forces an exhaustivity check at compile time, eliminating the legacy class of bug where a renderHandedness change could silently break this caller.
DB column for bat_side / pitch_hand is still Text (CHAR(1) has padding gotchas in PostgreSQL), but the API path is now total end-to-end.

decisions.name: IdempotencyByPayloadSha
decisions.what: syncRosters short-circuits when the inbound payloadSha matches the most recent fetch-log row for ('provider', 'active-rosters', 'scope'); the no-op path returns SyncResult { syncTeamsUpserted = 0, syncPlayersUpserted = 0, syncFetchSha256 = payloadSha } and emits one InfoS log line
why: Re-running with an unchanged payload should not re-upsert ~30 teams + ~700 players or write a new fetch-log row; that work is wasted writes and DB contention. The fetch-log already records payload_sha256 for exactly this purpose; the short-circuit reads at most one row before deciding whether to do anything.

Ordering is load-bearing: the fetch-log INSERT is the LAST step in the non-skip path, AFTER both upserts complete. A crash mid-upsert leaves no log row, so the next run retries rather than silently skips a partial state. Inverting this ordering would mask partial writes — comments at the call site flag this for future maintainers.
Phase C.1.

syncRosters.intent: Provider-agnostic upsert pipeline: SHA-checked short-circuit, then (on miss) teams, players, and finally a fetch-log entry
notes: single Clock.now call shared by both team and player upserts; both rows get identical last_synced_at
fetchLogResource hardcoded to 'active-rosters'; scope is supplied by the caller (typically the season as Text)
fetchLogRecordCount is the player count, NOT the team count; teams are bookkeeping
fetchLogId and fetchLogFetchedAt are Nothing on the inbound row; the DB layer fills them via DEFAULT

SHA short-circuit (Phase C.1): if payloadSha matches the most recent fetchLogRow.fetchLogPayloadSha256 for this (provider, 'active-rosters', scope), returns a zero-row SyncResult and emits exactly one InfoS log line. Both counts being zero is the canonical 'we skipped' signal — distinguishable from 'first call with empty inputs' by the syncFetchSha256 echoing the input
the fetch-log INSERT is the last step in the non-skip path; reordering it before the upserts would let a crash at the wrong moment silently mask a partial-state on the next run
consumes: CLI sync command (process startup or scheduled run)

upsertAllTeams: produces Map TeamId DbTeamId where the key is the upstream MLB id and the value is the surrogate DB id, in the order traverse visits the input list
extId = externalIdFromTeamId team — single source of truth for the encoding
teamRowId is Nothing on insert; the DB layer assigns the surrogate id
upsertAllPlayers: uses the team map from upsertAllTeams to resolve playerRowCurrentTeamId; players whose upstream team isn't in the map (unknown / minor league call-up) get Nothing for current_team_id
extId = externalIdFromPlayerId player — single source of truth
discards the DbPlayerId returned by upsertPlayerByExternalId; the caller doesn't need it
handedness conversion via handChar (total Domain function), not T.head of renderHandedness

decisions.name: SkipGamesWithUnknownTeams
decisions.what: syncSchedule resolves both away and home teams via lookupTeamByExternalId; if either is missing, the entire game is skipped and counted in schedGamesSkipped
why: The schedule endpoint can include teams that haven't been ingested yet (spring training affiliates, all-star game rosters, exhibition opponents).
Inserting a game with a NULL or fabricated team_id violates the foreign-key contract and silently corrupts later joins.
Skipping is recoverable: re-run after a roster sync and the game shows up. Failing the whole batch on one missing reference is not.
The skip count is surfaced in ScheduleSyncResult so operators can detect when this is happening at scale.

decisions.name: FetchLogResourceLiteralSchedule
decisions.what: syncSchedule writes fetchLogResource = 'schedule' as a literal rather than parameterising it
why: Mirrors the convention in Pelotero.Sync.Players where 'active-rosters' is the literal resource name.
If a future scope adds e.g. minor-league schedule fetches, that becomes a new resource string, not a flag here.

decisions.name: ExternalIdViaCentralisedHelper
decisions.what: upsertOneGame and resolveTeam call Pelotero.Provider.ExternalId helpers; no inline encoding
why: Phase A.1 made resolveTeam use externalIdFromTeamId on the lookup side and upsertOneGame use externalIdFromGameId for game external ids.

The implicit cross-module contract that previously lived in source comments ('the show-of-Int convention here MUST match upsertAllTeams') is now a typed function call. Source comments don't need to assert what the type system enforces.

decisions.name: IdempotencyByPayloadSha
decisions.what: syncSchedule short-circuits when the inbound payloadSha matches the most recent fetch-log row for ('provider', 'schedule', 'scope'); the no-op path returns ScheduleSyncResult { schedGamesUpserted = 0, schedGamesSkipped = 0, schedFetchSha256 = payloadSha } and emits one InfoS log line
why: Symmetric to the syncRosters short-circuit (Phase C.1). Re-running with an unchanged schedule payload should not re-upsert hundreds of games.
Ordering matters here too: the fetch-log INSERT is the LAST step in the non-skip path. A crash mid-upsert leaves no log row, so retry is safe.

Both counts (schedGamesUpserted and schedGamesSkipped) being zero is the unambiguous 'we skipped entirely' signal; distinguishable from a non-skip run with an empty input list because the input list of zero games is itself a degenerate non-skip case that still writes a fetch-log row.
Phase C.1.

syncSchedule.intent: Provider-agnostic upsert pipeline for already-converted [Game] domain values: SHA-checked short-circuit, then (on miss) per-game upserts and a fetch-log entry
notes: writes one fetch-log row per call (in the non-skip path) with resource = 'schedule', scope supplied by caller (typically a date-range string like '2025-04-01..2025-04-07')
fetchLogRecordCount is the total games count, NOT just upserted games; matches the input list length so an operator can compare against schedGamesUpserted to detect skip-rate
single Clock.now call shared across all game upserts in this run
iteration order is the input list order

SHA short-circuit (Phase C.1): if payloadSha matches the most recent fetchLogRow.fetchLogPayloadSha256 for this (provider, 'schedule', scope), returns a zero-row ScheduleSyncResult and emits exactly one InfoS log line. Both schedGamesUpserted and schedGamesSkipped are zero
the fetch-log INSERT is the last step in the non-skip path, mirroring syncRosters; this is load-bearing for partial-failure recovery

upsertOneGame: returns True on successful upsert, False on skip (either team unresolved)
discards the DbGameId returned by upsertGameByExternalId; downstream boxscore upserts re-resolve via lookupGameByExternalId at scoring time
resolveTeam: wraps lookupTeamByExternalId, calling externalIdFromTeamId for the encoding
the encoding is now type-checked at compile time via the Provider.ExternalId helper, not asserted via source comments

decisions.name: PerGameFetchLogEntry
decisions.what: syncBoxscores writes one FetchLogRow per game (resource = 'boxscore', scope = the GameId as text), not one row per batch
why: Catch-up runs ('which boxscores are new since last sync?') become a single getLastFetch query per gameId, which is the natural primitive for incremental work.
A per-batch row would force the caller to remember which games it included, defeating the purpose of an external log.
Cost: high write volume on a fresh-season backfill (~2400 rows for a full season). Acceptable; provider_fetch_log is append-only and not a query hot path.
Phase C.1 reads from this same per-game row to make the SHA short-circuit possible.

decisions.name: MissingPlayerSilentSkip
decisions.what: If lookupPlayerByExternalId returns Nothing for a boxscore entry's playerId, the entry is silently skipped (no upsert, no warning, no error)
why: Real cause: roster sync hasn't run for that player yet (mid-season callup, traded mid-game). Re-running after the next roster sync recovers the data.
Failing the whole game would lose 25 known-good batting lines because of one unknown player.
Trade-off: silently skipping means no operator visibility. A future improvement would be to count skipped entries in BoxscoreSyncResult so the operator can detect when this is happening at scale.

decisions.name: MissingTeamSilentDegradation
decisions.what: If a boxscore entry has a TeamId that isn't in the local DB, the team_id field is set to NULL rather than skipping the entry
why: The batting/pitching row is still useful without team attribution (player's stats are intact); team is a join convenience.
MLB occasionally ships parentTeamId values for teams that haven't been ingested (international roster expansions, mid-season ownership swaps).
Symmetrical to player handling above but lossier — at least the player would re-sync; an unknown team_id never gets backfilled. Worth flagging if it becomes common.

decisions.name: InningsPitchedOutsAtConvertTime
decisions.what: Conversion to outs happens in Pelotero.MLB.Convert.convertPitching at the wire boundary; pitchingRowFor in this module just copies pitOuts straight through
why: Phase B.1 moved the parse to convertPitching, where the wire string and the wire pitOuts are reconciled and a WireFieldDiscrepancy warning is emitted on disagreement. The sync layer no longer carries the redundancy; it sees a single Maybe Int.
Previously inningsPitchedOuts here did the prefer-IP-string-then-fall-back-to-outs dance. That logic is gone; this module is now a mechanical Int -> Int32 narrowing per field.

decisions.name: ExternalIdViaCentralisedHelper
decisions.what: syncOne uses externalIdFromGameId to resolve GameId -> DbGameId and externalIdFromPlayerId / externalIdFromTeamId for entry resolution
why: Phase A.1 unified the encoding; this module is one of the consumer sites. Same compile-time enforcement applies.
Phase C.1 also uses externalIdFromGameId as the fetch-log scope, so the SHA-lookup path goes through the same helper as the upsert path.

decisions.name: BoxscoreOutcomeTypedSum
decisions.what: syncOne returns Either BoxscoreSyncError BoxscoreOutcome where BoxscoreOutcome = BoxUpserted Int Int [ConvertWarning] | BoxUnchanged
why: Distinguishes 'fetched, parsed, upserted zero rows because the boxscore was genuinely empty' from 'short-circuited on SHA match because nothing changed since last run'. The two are operationally different and need different counters.
Replaces the prior (Int, Int, [ConvertWarning]) tuple. The aggregator in syncBoxscores increments boxGamesProcessed for BoxUpserted and boxGamesUnchanged for BoxUnchanged.
BoxUnchanged carries no warnings because no parse/convert ran; warnings are exclusively a parse/convert artefact.

decisions.name: IdempotencyByPayloadSha
decisions.what: syncOne computes sha256Hex of the fetched bytes, looks up the most recent fetch-log row for ('provider', 'boxscore', externalIdFromGameId gid), and returns BoxUnchanged if the SHA matches; in that case the parse, convert, upsert, and fetch-log INSERT are all skipped, and one InfoS log line is emitted
why: Asymmetry vs. syncRosters/syncSchedule: those callers compute the SHA before invoking the sync, so the short-circuit precedes the HTTP work entirely. For boxscores, the bytes are fetched inside syncOne via MLBClient, so the HTTP cost is unavoidable.

What the short-circuit saves is parse + convert + upsert + fetch-log INSERT — the bulk of the per-game DB work. For a fresh-season backfill where most games are already final (byte-identical on every refetch), this is one HTTP per game and zero DB work.
Live games (mid-game boxscores still updating) will never short-circuit because their bytes change on every poll. That is correct behaviour: live data has to be re-ingested.
Ordering remains load-bearing: the fetch-log INSERT is the LAST step of the non-skip path, so a crash mid-upsert leaves no log row and the next run retries.
Phase C.1.

syncBoxscores.intent: Process a list of upstream GameIds: resolve each to DbGameId, fetch raw boxscore bytes, decide via SHA whether the payload changed, then (on miss) decode, convert, and upsert per-player batting and pitching rows
notes: iterates input order; no concurrency at this layer
accumulates per-game results into a BoxscoreSyncResult so partial failures don't abort the batch
boxConvertWarnings is concatenated across all successfully-processed games (now includes any WireFieldDiscrepancy warnings from convertPitching); SHA-skipped games contribute no warnings
boxGamesSeen == boxGamesProcessed + boxGamesUnchanged + length boxErrors as an identity (modulo any future per-game skip categories tracked by boxGamesSkipped)

syncOne: GameNotKnown: lookupGameByExternalId returned Nothing; caller must run schedule sync first
FetchFailed: HTTP or transport-level failure from MLBClient
ParseFailed: Aeson decode failure on the raw bytes
writes FetchLog after a successful upsert pass, NOT before — a partial-write scenario doesn't get logged as a successful fetch

C.1 short-circuit: after a successful fetch but before parse, computes sha256Hex of the bytes and reads getLastFetch for ('provider', 'boxscore', externalIdFromGameId gid). On SHA match returns BoxUnchanged; otherwise proceeds with the original parse / convert / upsert / record-fetch path
upsertEntries: missing player -> skip entry (counts unchanged); missing team -> degrade team_id to NULL
boxBatting Nothing -> no batting row written; boxPitching Nothing -> no pitching row written
battingRowFor: mechanical Maybe Int -> Maybe Int32 widening for every stat field
pitchingRowFor: same as battingRowFor; pitOuts is passed straight through (no IP string reconciliation here post Phase B.1)
sha256Hex: raw ByteString -> hex-encoded Text via SHA-256

decisions.name: UrlsIsolatedAsSwapPoint
decisions.what: All MLB Stats API URLs live in this single module with no other logic; the only way to talk to the upstream service is via this module's exports
why: If MLB changes the API base or moves an endpoint, this is the only file that needs editing.
If a future provider replaces MLB entirely, this module is the natural delete-and-rewrite boundary.
Side effect: discourages ad-hoc URL construction scattered through fetch code.

rosterUrl: pre-filters to activeStatus=ACTIVE on the server side; inactive players are not returned
uses /sports/1/players (sport id 1 = MLB), not /people, because /people requires explicit ID lists
teamsUrl: uses sportId=1 (MLB) only; minor-league teams are not returned
scheduleUrl: language=en is hardcoded; the MLB API supports other locales but the engine doesn't model them
startDate and endDate are passed as raw String; caller is responsible for the YYYY-MM-DD format MLB expects
scheduleDateUrl: convenience wrapper for single-day queries; the MLB API does not have a separate per-day endpoint, so we issue a range query with start==end
boxscoreUrl: v1 endpoint; returns the boxscore object whose shape is parsed by Pelotero.MLB.Wire.Boxscore
gameStatusUrl: v1.1 endpoint (note the version difference from boxscoreUrl); /feed/live carries scheduled-vs-final status that the boxscore endpoint does not surface cleanly
currently UNUSED in the sync pipeline; reserved for the future 'is this game final yet?' check before scoring

decisions.name: WarningsBesideValuesNotInsteadOf
decisions.what: Conversion functions return ([ConvertWarning], Maybe a) or ([ConvertWarning], a) so warnings accumulate without halting the batch
why: MLB ships partial records during spring training; halting on the first one means losing the other 700 valid players.
Treating malformed records as exceptions would conflate parse errors (caught upstream by Aeson) with data-quality warnings (this layer's job).
The caller decides whether to log warnings, ignore them, or fail loudly via Logging.

decisions.name: MLBLooseDateFormat
decisions.what: parseDate uses '%Y-%-m-%-d' instead of '%Y-%m-%d'
why: MLB's schedule endpoint occasionally returns dates without zero-padding ('2024-3-5' instead of '2024-03-05').
The %-m / %-d directives accept both padded and unpadded forms.
Strict %m/%d would silently drop ~5% of pre-season games.

decisions.name: InvalidPlayerIdDropsRecord
decisions.what: convertPlayer drops players with id <= 0 entirely (returns Nothing) and emits an InvalidPlayerId warning
why: An id of 0 or negative is structurally meaningless; the surrogate-key lookup would fail and the rest of the row would be junk anyway.
Position and handedness warnings, in contrast, downgrade to Nothing for that field while keeping the rest of the player; the player is still useful as a name + team reference.
An invalid id removes the only stable identity the record has, so there is nothing left worth keeping.

decisions.name: BoxscoreEmitsDiscrepancyWarnings
decisions.what: convertBoxscore (specifically convertPitching) can now emit WireFieldDiscrepancy warnings when wire pitOuts disagrees with the parsed wire IP string
why: Phase B.1 moved IP-string reconciliation here. We parse both wbpInningsPitched and wbpOuts, compare them, and emit WireFieldDiscrepancy if they disagree (rare; usually only during live-update windows).
Output remains a single Maybe Int via parseInningsPitched ip <|> wbpOuts: parsed string is preferred (canonical), wire outs is a fallback, both Nothing is preserved.
Boxscore conversion previously never emitted warnings (the BoxscoreNeverWarns decision); that decision is now narrowed to the batting path. Pitching can warn; batting still doesn't.

decisions.name: DateParseFailureSilentlyDropsEntireDate
decisions.what: convertDateEntry returns ([], []) on date parse failure without emitting an InvalidGameDate warning
why: InvalidGameDate is a defined ConvertWarning constructor but no current code path produces one — it exists for the rendering pass and as an extension point.
Real MLB dates parse via the loose-padding format; failure here would indicate a structural feed change, not a data-quality issue worth surfacing per game.
Known gap: a date corruption in one entry silently loses an entire day's games. Documented as a known limitation.

renderWarning: renders each ConvertWarning constructor as a single line of stable text
format is conventional: 'convert: <subject> <id> <verb> <detail>'; downstream log scrapers can rely on the leading 'convert: ' prefix
tshow uses Show on the int id, so player ids appear without quotes
WireFieldDiscrepancy renders as 'convert: pitching <playerId> wire field discrepancy: ip=<text> outs=<int>'
convertPlayer: returns ([InvalidPlayerId], Nothing) for ids <= 0; the empty-warning case never produces Nothing here
useName / useLastName / nameSlug all default to T.empty when absent (orEmpty); the DB schema requires NOT NULL, so empty is the safe default
playerActive is non-optional in the wire shape; if MLB ever drops it, parsing breaks at Aeson level, not here
currentTeam is decoded as Maybe; teamless players (free agents, just-released) get Nothing for playerTeamId
convertPlayers: concats per-player warnings; the resulting list is in input order (well-defined because the envelope's player list is a list)
uses mapMaybe to filter out the Nothing cases (invalid ids); does NOT preserve a placeholder for them

notes: tries abbreviation first, then code; if both are present and one parses while the other is unknown, prefers the parsed one without warning
if NEITHER parses but at least one is present, emits UnknownPosition with the abbreviation if available else the code
if both are Nothing, returns ([], Nothing) silently — the position field is genuinely optional for some records

convertHand: WireHandRef wraps a Maybe Text; this function handles WireHandRef Nothing (silent), WireHandRef (Just code) parseable (silent), and WireHandRef (Just code) unknown (warning)
no validation that batSide and pitchHand are consistent for switch-hitters; they are independent fields
convertSchedule: folds over wseDates building (warnings, games) in date order
produces GameSchedule wrapping a flat [Game]; the per-date grouping in the wire format is discarded
off-days and missing date entries simply produce no games and no warnings
convertDateEntry: if the date string fails parseDate the WHOLE date entry is dropped silently — see decision DateParseFailureSilentlyDropsEntireDate
wdeGames Nothing means 'no games scheduled'; treated as []
delegates per-game conversion to convertGame which then attaches its own warnings
convertGame: extracts away/home team ids from the wire's nested teams.away.team.id and teams.home.team.id
if either is missing, emits MissingTeamRef with the gamePk and returns Nothing for the game
preserves the gameDate by carrying the parsed Day in from convertDateEntry
parseDate: returns Nothing for any unparseable input; never throws
convertBoxscore: returns ([WireFieldDiscrepancy], entries); the only warnings produced here come from convertPitching
concatenates away-side then home-side entries; team identification on each entry uses wbpParentTeamId from the wire
the GameId comes from the caller
boxsideEntries: iterates Map.elems of the players map; the wire keys ('ID660271') are discarded
missing batting or pitching stats default to emptyBatting / emptyPitching
convertBatting: mechanical field-by-field copy from WireBoxBatting to BattingStats; no derivation, parsing, or fallback
any divergence between the two record shapes is a compile error here

convertPitching.intent: Convert WireBoxPitching to PitchingStats, reconciling wire IP string against wire outs and emitting a WireFieldDiscrepancy if they disagree
notes: parses wbpInningsPitched via parseInningsPitched; compares against wbpOuts when both are present
on disagreement: emits WireFieldDiscrepancy and prefers the parsed IP string
output pitOuts = parseInningsPitched ip <|> wbpOuts (parsed string preferred, wire outs fallback)
every other field is a mechanical copy

orEmpty: Maybe Text -> Text helper, falling back to T.empty
used to avoid scattering 'fromMaybe T.empty' through the conversion code
tshow: used in renderWarning to embed numeric ids in messages

decisions.name: WireToDomainTeamPrivate
decisions.what: wireToDomainTeam is not exported; it is duplicated by hand in Pelotero.Effects.MLBClient
why: Exporting it would create a circular concern: Fetch shouldn't be a public utility module, it's the production HTTP path.
The conversion is one record literal with four fields; duplicating it is cheaper than the import discipline of having both Fetch and MLBClient depend on a shared private module.
If a third caller appears, this should move to a Convert-level helper.

decisions.name: PayloadShaIsTeamsBytesThenPlayersBytes
decisions.what: computeSha hashes the concatenation of teamsBody (raw bytes) followed by playersBody (raw bytes), in that order
why: Order matters for stability: if a future fetch reorders the calls, a re-fetch with identical content would produce a different SHA, breaking change-detection.
Using the lazy-then-strict transform inside fetchRosters is a one-place implementation detail and not part of the SHA's semantics.
Teams-then-players matches the order they're parsed and converted in the same function.

fetchRosters.intent: Real-HTTP roster fetcher: pulls teams and players, parses both, converts to domain, returns FetchedRosters with payload SHA
notes: two HTTP calls happen sequentially, not concurrently; latency is teams + players, not max(teams, players)
if either fetch errors at HTTP level, returns Left with the URL in the message
if either body fails to parse (Aeson), returns Left with 'Teams parse failure: ...' or 'Players parse failure: ...' prefix
warnings from convertPlayers are surfaced in frWarnings; team conversion does not produce warnings
frPayloadSha is over the concatenation of raw response bodies

wireToDomainTeam: wtLocationName is Maybe Text in the wire; defaults to T.empty because Team.teamLocationName is non-Maybe

fetchSchedule.intent: Real-HTTP schedule fetcher for a date range
notes: single HTTP call; parses through Pelotero.MLB.Wire.Schedule then converts via Convert.convertSchedule
warnings are passed through as fsWarnings
returns Left on HTTP error or parse failure

fetchBoxscoreRaw: returns the raw response body as ByteString without parsing
the caller parses with Pelotero.MLB.Wire.Boxscore + Pelotero.MLB.Convert.convertBoxscore at the point of use
asymmetry vs. fetchRosters/fetchSchedule is deliberate: boxscore fetches are sometimes archived raw before processing
fetchUrl: private helper; one HTTP GET, returns the body or an HTTP error message
non-2xx responses are returned as Left, not thrown
computeSha: SHA-256 of the input bytes, hex-encoded as Text

decisions.name: FlatRecordPerStatsCategory
decisions.what: The batting and pitching wire records list every Maybe Int field individually rather than using a Map Text Int
why: Named fields make the conversion to BattingStats / PitchingStats a mechanical record-to-record copy that the compiler verifies.
A Map-based representation would defer typo-detection to runtime.
The cost is verbose Aeson FromJSON instances, but those are write-once.

decisions.name: InningsPitchedAsTextAtWireOnly
decisions.what: wbpInningsPitched is decoded as Maybe Text; wbpOuts is decoded as Maybe Int; both stay as wire-shape, with reconciliation in convertPitching
why: MLB sends '6.2' meaning six and two-thirds innings; decoding as Double gives floating-point grief.
Both fields persist all the way to convertPitching, where they are reconciled and a discrepancy warning is emitted on disagreement.
After Phase B.1, the Domain.Stats type stores ONLY pitOuts. The Text representation is a wire-layer fact only.

decisions.name: WireTeamMinimalFields
decisions.what: WireTeam parses only id, name, abbreviation, and locationName; ignores division, league, venue, founded year, etc.
why: The DB stores only what we display in lineup/box rendering; ignoring the rest is the simplest way to avoid schema bloat.
If a future feature needs division or league info, we re-parse here without any data migration.
Aeson silently ignores unknown JSON keys, so this is forward-compatible against MLB adding fields.

decisions.name: InlineWireGameTeamParser
decisions.what: WireGameTeam's FromJSON instance manually extracts team.id rather than reusing WireTeamRef from Wire.Player
why: Schedule context only needs the id; pulling in WireTeamRef would either re-export it from Player.hs or duplicate the type.
Inlining the parse keeps the Schedule wire module self-contained.
If schedule entries ever need team names, this is the place to swap in WireTeamRef.

decisions.name: TolerantParseStrictRender
decisions.what: parseProviderName returns Maybe rather than failing; renderProviderName is total over the closed sum
why: Reading: an unknown provider name in the database (e.g. an old row from a discontinued provider) shouldn't crash the whole query.
Writing: the writer always uses the rendered constant from the sum, so writes are never typos.
Adding a provider is a code change (new constructor + new parse case + new render case); no migration needed because the column is TEXT.

decisions.name: WireFormatNamesAreStable
decisions.what: renderProviderName values ('mlb', 'pelotero-internal') are stable strings that can never change without a data migration
why: The text is stored in DB rows (player_external_id, team_external_id, game_external_id, provider_fetch_log).
Renaming a constructor without renaming the rendered string would silently invalidate every row of that provider.

renderProviderName: exhaustive over the sum; adding a constructor without a render case is a -Wincomplete-patterns error
produces lowercase, hyphen-separated names matching the SQL convention
parseProviderName: returns Nothing for unknown names rather than failing
case-sensitive: 'MLB' and 'mlb' are distinct, only the second matches

decisions.name: ParametricExternalIdEntity
decisions.what: ExternalIdE i f is a single rel8able record parameterised by the surrogate id type, NOT three separate per-table records (PlayerExternalId, TeamExternalId, GameExternalId)
why: All three external-id companion tables have identical column shape (entity_id, provider, external_id, fetched_at); the only difference is the type of entity_id. Sharing the record type forces that fact at compile time.
Adding a fourth provider-keyed table is one TableSchema literal plus one ProviderKeyed instance; no new entity record needed.
Cost: one Rel8able instance with a (DBType i, DBEq i) constraint, plus standalone-deriving ergonomics. Acceptable for the consolidation.

decisions.name: TypeclassOverRecordOfFunctions
decisions.what: ProviderKeyed is a typeclass with associated type families (RowEntity, RowId), not a record-of-functions value passed to free-standing helpers
why: The associated type families let GHC propagate RowId row through to the surrogate-id type at every call site without manual threading.
Type applications (linkExternalIdT @PlayerRow) at the few sites where row is otherwise ambiguous from the value-level args; explicit and greppable.
A Proxy-based or record-of-functions variant would push that disambiguation to value-level boilerplate at every call site.

decisions.name: InsertAndUpdateAreInstanceMethods
decisions.what: insertRowT and updateRowByIdT are typeclass methods (each instance provides its own), NOT default methods derived from rowSchema and a generic rowToExpr
why: The rel8 Insert and Update clauses need entity-specific knowledge: which field is the surrogate id (so it can be set to unsafeDefault on insert and to lit pid on update), and the per-field 'lit value' translation. Generalising this would require per-field traversals via Generic, which is more machinery than the three current callers justify.
Each instance's insertRowT and updateRowByIdT are literally one-liners that point at the existing per-table insertXxxT and updateXxxT functions, so no real boilerplate is added.
If a fourth provider-keyed table arrives, this design extends cleanly: write the per-table insert/update, declare the instance.

decisions.name: FacadesPreserveCallSites
decisions.what: Per-table modules (Pelotero.DB.Player / .Team / .Game) re-export the four external-id helpers and their Pool wrappers as one-line facades that call PK.foo @MyRow
why: Zero call-site changes outside the DB layer. The effect interpreters (runPlayersDB etc.) and Sync code keep importing Pelotero.DB.Player.upsertByExternalIdT exactly as before.
Cost: 4 × 2 = 8 trivial wrapper definitions per table. Worth it to keep the migration scope narrow.
If we later decide call sites should go through PK directly, deleting the facades is a mechanical follow-up.

linkExternalIdT: INSERT into externalIdSchema with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING; idempotent on re-runs
_eidFetchedAt set via unsafeDefault — the DB column has DEFAULT NOW()
lookupByExternalIdT: SELECT _eidEntityId WHERE provider AND external_id; returns the first row or Nothing
Phase A.5: replaces the inline lookup that was duplicated across DB.Player / DB.Team / DB.Game
getExternalIdT: Reverse lookup; SELECT _eidExternalId WHERE entity_id AND provider
upsertByExternalIdT: Atomic within the caller's transaction: lookupByExternalIdT, then either updateRowByIdT (existing entity) or insertRowT + linkExternalIdT (new entity)
Returns the surrogate id either way — caller doesn't need to distinguish insert vs. update

decisions.name: DefaultsAreLocalDevValues
decisions.what: defaultDBConfig points at localhost:5433 / pelotero-engine with empty user/password
why: These are values for the local Nix dev shell; they fail loudly if used in production.
Production setups must set PG* env vars; sops-nix handles this in real deploys.
An alternative was to require all values explicitly, but that breaks 'cabal run' in a dev shell where defaults are convenient.

decisions.name: DbErrorIsTypedSum
decisions.what: PoolUsageError and MigrationError are constructors of a pure Haskell DBError; consumers can pattern-match rather than re-parse a rendered string
why: Phase A.3 made DBError flow through the effect layer as a typed Error co-effect; callers in tests or in CLI commands that care about specific failure modes (pool exhaustion, migration drift) can match on the constructor.
renderDBError is still the canonical user-facing rendering; the type is just no longer opaque-text-only.
Adding a new error category remains a constructor + a renderDBError case.

defaultDBConfig: host=localhost, port=5433, db=pelotero-engine, empty user/password, pool=10, timeout=10s
matches Nix dev shell launch script defaults

loadDBConfig.intent: Read DB config from libpq-conventional env vars + two pelotero-specific tunables
notes: PGHOST/PGPORT/PGDATABASE/PGUSER/PGPASSWORD: standard libpq names
PELOTERO_DB_POOL_SIZE / PELOTERO_DB_ACQUIRE_TIMEOUT: app-specific tunables
missing or unparseable env vars fall back to defaultDBConfig field-by-field

poolConfig: private; constructs PoolConfig.Config from a DBConfig
acquire: non-blocking; returns immediately. Pool only opens connections lazily on first runSession.
no validation that the database is reachable until first use
release: drains the pool; safe to call on a partially-used pool
does NOT abort in-flight transactions; finishes them then closes connections
runSession: wraps Pool.use; converts hasql-pool errors to DBError
preserves the Right value type a as-is
runTransaction: convenience wrapper: ReadCommitted, Write, single Transaction
atomicity: write commits on success, rolls back on Tx error or thrown exception
renderDBError: converts to user-facing Text with a category prefix ('DB pool usage error: ', 'Migration error: ')

decisions.name: OwnedMigrationRunner
decisions.what: Custom migration runner instead of hasql-migration
why: hasql-migration is broken against current crypton (which we use for SHA-256) and is effectively unmaintained.
Migrations are a couple hundred lines we can own outright; less cost than maintaining a fork.
Owning the implementation also lets us encode our specific operational policy (immutable migrations, hash mismatch is a hard error) directly.

decisions.name: ImmutableMigrationsHashChecked
decisions.what: Each migration file is hashed (SHA-256) on first apply; subsequent runs verify the hash and abort with Mismatch if the file has changed
why: Prevents accidental edits from silently de-syncing dev/prod schemas.
Forces the convention 'create a new V0042__ file' rather than 'edit V0007__'.
Whitespace-sensitive on purpose: any edit, even cosmetic, trips the alarm.

decisions.name: PerMigrationTransaction
decisions.what: Each migration runs in its own transaction (not the whole batch)
why: A failure rolls back exactly the offending migration, leaving the prior ones intact.
Avoids the 'partially applied batch' state.

decisions.name: FilenameOrderIsApplyOrder
decisions.what: Migration files are sorted lexicographically; apply order = filename order
why: The convention V<NNNN>__<desc>.sql with zero-padded numbers makes lexicographic order match numeric order.
Forgetting to zero-pad (V42__ before V9__) is caught by code review, not by the runner.

runMigrations.intent: Apply all .sql files in dir that haven't been applied; verify checksums of those that have
notes: missing directory is a hard error (MigrationError 'Migration directory not found')
SUCCESS path: returns Right MigrationOutcome with totals
MISMATCH path: returns Left MigrationError with the filename
ensures schema_migrations exists via a CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS at the start of applyAll
idempotent: safe to call on every process startup
most recent migration: V0030__lineup_snapshot.sql (added in Phase B.3)

loadScript: private; reads a file's bytes and computes its SHA-256 hex string
scriptName is the bare filename (Text), not the full path
applyAll: first runs ensureMigrationsTable in its own transaction
then folds over scripts; on the first Mismatch, stops and returns Left
applyOne: looks up the prior checksum for this filename; if present and matching, returns Skipped
if present and DIFFERENT, returns Mismatch (does NOT throw — the caller decides)
if absent, runs the SQL via Tx.sql then inserts the (filename, checksum) pair, both in the same transaction
ensureMigrationsTable: CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS schema_migrations (filename TEXT PK, checksum TEXT NOT NULL, applied_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW())
selectChecksum: Statement Text -> Maybe Text; one row or none
hexSha256: ByteString -> Text; SHA-256 then base16 then UTF-8 decode

decisions.name: OrphanInstancesAreDeliberate
decisions.what: DBType / DBEq / DBOrd instances for domain id types live here as orphans; the {-# OPTIONS_GHC -Wno-orphans #-} pragma is intentional
why: Putting them in Pelotero.Domain.Id forces the domain layer to depend on rel8, which is the wrong direction.
Putting them in each Pelotero.DB.* table module produces orphan-conflict warnings as soon as two table modules reference the same domain type.
This module is the lowest place that already imports both the domain types and rel8.
Importers use the empty-import idiom: 'import Pelotero.DB.Rel8Instances ()'.

decisions.name: JsonbInstancesOnDomainTypes
decisions.what: ToJSON / FromJSON instances for LeagueScoring / RosterLimits / LineupLimits / batting and pitching multipliers live on the Domain types directly today; the rel8 JSONBEncoded deriving via dispatches through those instances
why: This is the wrong-direction layering (Domain depends on Aeson) but is the current state. The planned A.4 work moves these instances onto newtype wrappers in a Pelotero.DB.JsonB module so Domain becomes Aeson-free.
Deferring A.4 keeps this module simple at the cost of the layering smell.

decisions.name: ProviderNameTextEnumDb
decisions.what: ProviderName decodes via parseTypeInformation, with parseProviderName as the decoder; on unknown values it returns Left, which becomes a hasql query failure
why: Unlike Pelotero.DB.FetchLog.fromResult (which decodes to Maybe and filters), this DBType instance is strict.
Tables that use ProviderName directly must only contain known providers, OR the table must decode to Text and convert in code.
This asymmetry is per-table by design: external-id tables are write-controlled; the fetch log is append-only and historical.

decisions.name: TwoTablePlayerExternalIdSplit
decisions.what: player table holds the canonical row; player_external_id holds (player_id, provider, external_id) tuples
why: A player can have ids from multiple providers without schema gymnastics on the player table.
If a player gets re-identified, the player row stays put; only the external_id rows update.
Cost: every upsert is two operations; the boilerplate currently lives per-table here, in Pelotero.DB.Team, and in Pelotero.DB.Game (planned A.5 collapses this into a typeclass).

decisions.name: BatHandStoredAsText
decisions.what: DB column for bat_side / pitch_hand is Text; the API exposes Char
why: PostgreSQL doesn't have a native single-character type smaller than TEXT (CHAR(1) exists but has fixed-length-padding gotchas).
Char in Haskell is multi-byte (Unicode) so storing as Text is structurally correct.
API uses Char because the only legal values are 'L', 'R', 'S' and a Char is the most precise way to encode 'exactly one character of these three'.
Conversion API is now total at the Domain layer (handChar) post Phase A.6; this module only does the Text<->Char shuffle which remains structurally honest.

playerSchema: table 'player' with surrogate id, denormalised name, position, batting/pitching hand as text, active flag, FK to team, last-synced metadata
playerCurrentTeamId is Maybe DbTeamId; a player without a team has NULL
charToText: Maybe Char -> Maybe Text via T.singleton; preserves None
textToChar: Maybe Text -> Maybe Char via T.uncons
if the stored text has more than one character (data corruption), silently truncates
fromResult: private; converts the rel8 Player Result row to the public PlayerRow
insertPlayerT: INSERT ... RETURNING id; uses Abort on conflict
the surrogate id is unsafeDefault (DB-assigned BIGSERIAL); all other fields come from the row
updatePlayerT: WHERE id = pid; updates everything except id
getByIdT: single-row select via WHERE; returns the first match or Nothing
getAllT: ORDER BY last_name, first_name; returns the entire table
getActiveT: ORDER BY last_name, first_name; WHERE active = TRUE
linkExternalIdT: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING into player_external_id
idempotent; safe to call repeatedly during re-syncs
lookupByExternalIdT: SELECT player_id WHERE provider AND external_id; returns Maybe DbPlayerId
getExternalIdT: reverse lookup: given a DbPlayerId and provider, returns Maybe Text
upsertByExternalIdT: two-step: lookup via (provider, external_id); if found, update player; if not, insert and link

decisions.name: MirrorsPlayerSchema
decisions.what: team and team_external_id mirror the shape of player and player_external_id
why: Same provider-keyed pattern as Player. The duplication between this module and Pelotero.DB.Player is the structural cost of separate FK companion tables; planned A.5 work collapses the duplicate boilerplate into a typeclass.

teamSchema: table 'team' with surrogate id, name, abbreviation, location_name (city), and last-synced metadata
no FK out — teams are leaves in the FK graph
teamExternalIdSchema: same shape as player_external_id: (team_id, provider, external_id, fetched_at)
insertTeamT: INSERT ... RETURNING id; Abort on conflict
updateTeamT: WHERE id = tid; updates everything except id
getAllT: ORDER BY name; no pagination; 30 MLB teams
linkExternalIdT: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING into team_external_id
lookupByExternalIdT: SELECT team_id WHERE provider AND external_id

decisions.name: GameDateAsDay
decisions.what: game.game_date stores Day (no time of day), not UTCTime
why: Fantasy scoring periods are defined by date in the league's local timezone; game start times within a day are irrelevant for whether the game counts.
Storing as TIMESTAMPTZ would force every query to deal with timezone offset for what is fundamentally a calendar question.

decisions.name: MirrorsTeamSchema
decisions.what: game and game_external_id mirror the shape of team and team_external_id
why: Same provider-keyed pattern as Player and Team. Planned A.5 work collapses the duplicate boilerplate.

gameSchema: table 'game' with surrogate id, game_date (Day), away/home team FKs to team.id, last-synced metadata
gameExternalIdSchema: same shape as player_external_id and team_external_id
getByDateRangeT: WHERE game_date BETWEEN startDay AND endDay (inclusive both ends)
ORDER BY game_date ASC, id ASC for stable cross-day display
getByDateRange: Pool-flavored wrapper; inclusive on both ends
insertGameT: INSERT ... RETURNING id; Abort on conflict
updateGameT: WHERE id = gid; updates everything except id
linkExternalIdT: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING into game_external_id
lookupByExternalIdT: SELECT game_id WHERE provider AND external_id

decisions.name: ProviderColumnIsTextNotEnum
decisions.what: _flProvider is Column f Text, NOT Column f ProviderName
why: The fetch log is append-only and historical; a row written by a provider that no longer exists must remain readable.
If we used the ProviderName DBType (which fails on unknown values), a single legacy row would crash every fetch-log query.
fromResult does the parse and returns Nothing for unparseable rows; getLastFetchT and getRecentFetchesT use mapMaybe to drop them silently.

decisions.name: RecordCountAsInt32
decisions.what: fetchLogRecordCount is Int32, not Int64 or Int
why: INTEGER (not BIGINT) in PostgreSQL; 2^31 ~= 2 billion records per fetch is plenty.
Using Int (machine-word) would silently widen on 64-bit platforms, then narrow at the wire boundary.

fetchLogSchema: table 'provider_fetch_log' with id (BIGSERIAL), provider (TEXT), resource, scope, fetched_at, payload_sha256, record_count (INTEGER)
fromResult: Returns Nothing if _flProvider doesn't parse as a known ProviderName
recordFetchT: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT Abort; the fetch log is append-only
getLastFetchT: ORDER BY fetched_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 1; the id-DESC tiebreaker handles same-millisecond fetches
getRecentFetchesT: same ORDER BY pattern, LIMIT lim; returns up to `lim` parseable rows

decisions.name: ScoringAndLimitsAsJsonbColumns
decisions.what: scoring_config (JSONB), roster_limits (JSONB), and lineup_limits (JSONB) are columns whose Aeson instances live on the underlying Domain types (LeagueScoring, RosterLimits, LineupLimits)
why: JSONB lets us evolve the inner record shape without a schema migration on every existing row.
Domain types currently carry the ToJSON/FromJSON instances directly. This is the wrong-direction layering (Domain depends on Aeson) and is the planned A.4 work to fix via newtype wrappers.

decisions.name: StatusAsTextNotEnum
decisions.what: _lcStatus is Column f Text, not the LeagueStatus domain sum
why: Same rationale as ProviderName for the fetch log: tolerate legacy or unrecognised values without crashing reads.
The layered domain type LeagueStatus exists as the canonical render/parse pair; this column being Text is the persistence-layer trade-off.

leagueConfigSchema: table 'league_config' with surrogate id, league_id (Text), commissioner, status, JSONB scoring/roster/lineup, draft params, scoring period bounds
insertLeagueConfigT: INSERT ... RETURNING id; Abort on conflict
updateLeagueConfigT: WHERE id = lcid; updates everything except id

decisions.name: TeamKeySeparateFromName
decisions.what: league_team has both team_key (stable identifier within a league) and name (mutable display name)
why: Owners change team names mid-season; references from elsewhere (rosters, lineups, picks) must remain stable.
team_key is the join key; name is the rendered string.
(league_config_id, team_key) is the natural compound key.

leagueTeamSchema: table 'league_team' with surrogate id, FK to league_config, team_key (stable), name, owner
no last-synced metadata — league teams are user-managed, not externally synced
insertLeagueTeamT: INSERT ... RETURNING id; Abort on conflict
updateLeagueTeamT: WHERE id = ltid; updates everything except id
lookupByKeyT: WHERE league_config_id AND team_key; returns the first match or Nothing
getForLeagueT: ORDER BY name; all teams in a league
deleteT: DELETE WHERE id; cascading deletes on dependent rows handled by FK ON DELETE

decisions.name: UpsertOnPlayerNotSlot
decisions.what: addSlotT does ON CONFLICT (league_team_id, player_id) DO UPDATE SET slot, NOT (league_team_id, slot)
why: The natural-feeling 'a slot can hold one player' is wrong for fantasy; multiple OF/UTIL slots per team is normal.
The actual invariant is 'a player is in at most one slot per team'.
Adding a player who's already on the roster moves them to the new slot rather than failing or duplicating.

rosterSlotSchema: table 'roster_slot' with surrogate id, FK to league_team, slot (Text), FK to player, created_at
no order_index column today; planned B.2 work adds it for batting-order positional persistence
fromResult: private; drops the hidden surrogate id and created_at
addSlotT: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (league_team_id, player_id) DO UPDATE SET slot
getSlotsForTeamT: WHERE league_team_id; ORDER BY slot, player_id
replaceTeamRosterT: transaction-internal sequence: clearTeamRosterT then mapM_ addSlotT

decisions.name: MirrorsRosterSlotShape
decisions.what: lineup_slot is structurally identical to roster_slot
why: Lineups and rosters are different concepts but the storage shape stays parallel.
Same caveat as roster_slot: no order_index today; planned B.2 work adds it on both tables in one migration.

lineupSlotSchema: table 'lineup_slot' with surrogate id, FK to league_team, slot (Text), FK to player, created_at
no order_index column today; see B.2 in RosterSlot
fromResult: private; same omission of id and created_at as RosterSlot.fromResult
getSlotsForTeamT: WHERE league_team_id; ORDER BY slot, player_id

decisions.name: SnapshotKeyedByLeagueTeamAndGame
decisions.what: lineup_snapshot has UNIQUE (league_team_id, game_id, slot, player_id); a snapshot is the team's lineup-as-of-this-specific-game
why: Phase B.3 introduced the table to fix the correctness bug where scoring used current lineups against historical games.
(league_team_id, game_id) is the lookup key for scoring; slot + player_id complete the row's identity.
snapshotted_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW() records when the snapshot was actually taken; useful for debugging late-snapshot or out-of-order-snapshot scenarios.
No order_index column today; if/when B.2 adds it to lineup_slot, the snapshot will need it too so that snapshots preserve the lineup ordering at snapshot time.

decisions.name: ImmutableSnapshotsViaOnConflictDoNothing
decisions.what: writeSnapshotsT uses ON CONFLICT (league_team_id, game_id, slot, player_id) DO NOTHING; once a snapshot row exists, it is never overwritten
why: Snapshots model 'the lineup at game start' and must be immutable after that.
Combined with Lineup.Snapshot's pre-check via snapshotExistsForTeamGameT, this gives 'first snapshot wins' semantics for the (team, game) pair as a whole.
Re-running snapshot jobs is therefore a safe operational primitive.

lineupSnapshotSchema: table 'lineup_snapshot' with id (BIGSERIAL), league_team_id (FK), game_id (FK), slot (Text), player_id (FK), snapshotted_at (TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW())
fromResult: drops surrogate id and snapshotted_at from the public row type
writeSnapshotsT: INSERT [LineupSnapshotRow] ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING; returns ()
empty input returns immediately without hitting the database
callers track the count of attempted rows via 'length' on the input; the function does not return a count today
getSnapshotForTeamGameT: WHERE league_team_id AND game_id; no SQL-level ordering
consumed by Pelotero.Score.scoreTeamForGame (the canonical scoring read)
snapshotExistsForTeamGameT: SELECT ... LIMIT 1; returns True iff at least one row exists for the (team, game) pair
used by Pelotero.Lineup.Snapshot.snapshotLineupsForTeam as the 'is this snapshot already locked in?' guard
getSnapshotsForGameT: WHERE game_id; returns every snapshot row across all teams for one game
useful for debugging or auditing; not on the scoring hot path

decisions.name: NoSurrogateIdNaturalKey
decisions.what: player_ranking has no surrogate id; (league_team_id, player_id) is the primary key
why: Unlike roster_slot/lineup_slot where the (team, player) pair has a 'context' (the slot string), a ranking pair carries only its rank_slot integer.
Fewer columns, simpler schema.

decisions.name: AbortOnConflictForRankings
decisions.what: insertOneT uses Abort, not Upsert; replaceRankingsT works by clear-then-fill
why: Rankings are typically replaced wholesale rather than tweaked incrementally.
Abort + clear-then-fill is conceptually simpler than upsert.

playerRankingSchema: table 'player_ranking' with FK to league_team, FK to player, rank_slot (Int32), updated_at
PK is (league_team_id, player_id) — no surrogate id
fromResult: private; rel8 Result -> PlayerRankingRow; drops updated_at
getRankingsForTeamT: intended consumer is the planned Pelotero.Draft state machine (D.1); no consumer in tree today

decisions.name: AppendOnlyDraftPicks
decisions.what: Only insert (recordPick) and read (getPicksForLeague, getPickCount) operations exist; no update or delete
why: Picks are historical events; once made, they don't get edited or undone.
If a wrong pick needs correction, the convention is to insert a new pick at the next pick_number rather than mutating the prior row.
Audit trail integrity: a query at any point in time gives the actual sequence of picks made.

draftPickSchema: table 'draft_pick' with surrogate id, FK to league_config, pick_number (Int32 — 1-indexed), FK to league_team, FK to player, picked_at
recordPickT: INSERT ... RETURNING id; Abort on conflict
intended consumer is the planned Pelotero.Draft state machine (D.1); no consumer in tree today
getPickCountT: used to figure out 'whose pick is next?' as count + 1

decisions.name: TwoTablesNotOne
decisions.what: Batting and pitching are separate tables (game_player_batting and game_player_pitching), not one wide table
why: Batting has ~25 stat columns, pitching has ~40. Combining gives a 65-column row that's mostly NULL for any given player.
Querying 'all batting lines this week' becomes a clean SELECT from one table without WHERE filtering on column NULLness.
A two-way player gets two rows, one per table — correct because both stat lines are independently meaningful.

decisions.name: InningsPitchedAsOuts
decisions.what: The pitching table stores INTEGER outs, NOT the wire string '6.2'
why: Storing as outs makes SUM, AVG, and arithmetic exact; a decimal column would lose precision.
Conversion happens at convert time in Pelotero.MLB.Convert.convertPitching (Phase B.1); readers always see exact integer outs.
Domain.Stats.PitchingStats now also has only pitOuts (Phase B.1 dropped pitInningsPitched), so the DB row, the domain row, and the scoring path all agree.

decisions.name: UpdatedAtFromSqlNow
decisions.what: Upsert sets updated_at = RT.now (a SQL-side NOW()), preserving created_at from the existing row
why: RT.now is rel8's Expr-level NOW() — runs at DB transaction time, not at Haskell wall-clock time.
Taking the timestamp client-side would risk skew between client and DB clocks.

battingSchema: table 'game_player_batting' with FK to game, FK to player, FK to team (nullable), 25 stat columns (all Maybe Int32), created_at, updated_at
pitchingSchema: table 'game_player_pitching' with FK to game, FK to player, FK to team (nullable), 40+ stat columns, innings_pitched_outs as Int32, created_at, updated_at
fromBattingResult: private; rel8 BattingE Result -> BattingRow; drops created_at and updated_at
fromPitchingResult: private; rel8 PitchingE Result -> PitchingRow; drops created_at and updated_at
battingRowToExpr: private; BattingRow -> BattingE Expr for use in INSERT VALUES clause
created_at and updated_at are unsafeDefault — DB sets them on insert
upsertBattingT: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (game_id, player_id) DO UPDATE
set: keeps id-like columns from old, takes stats from new, preserves created_at, sets updated_at = NOW()
updateWhere = lit True (always update on conflict)
getBattingForGameT: consumed by Pelotero.Score.buildPlayerMaps (one call per game id in the period)
deleteBattingForGameT: useful when re-ingesting a corrected boxscore

decisions.name: OneOperationOneTransaction
decisions.what: Database has a single operation, runTx, which acquires a connection and runs the transaction in isolation
why: Each runTx is its own atomic unit; no need for callers to manage connection scope.
Composing multiple runTx calls is NOT one transaction — they're independent. If you need a multi-step atomic operation, build a single Transaction and pass it to one runTx.
This matches Pool.runTransaction's contract; the Database effect is a thin wrapper to make it dispatchable through the effectful machinery.

decisions.name: DbErrorAsTypedCoEffect
decisions.what: runDatabasePool requires Logging and Error DBError co-effects; DBErrors flow through the effect system as typed errors and are also logged at ErrorS before throwing
why: Phase A.3 replaced the runOrThrow pattern. Callers that don't care about typed handling do `runErrorNoCallStack @DBError` at the top of the program and either crash or log on Left; callers that want to handle pool exhaustion specifically can pattern-match on PoolUsageError.
Removes the lossy `show` step that used to live in runOrThrow; structured error data now propagates intact.
Logging the error before throwing means a silently-discarded Left still leaves a trace.

Every effect runner consuming Database (Players, Teams, Games, BoxscoreEntry, FetchLog, LeagueConfig, LeagueTeam, RosterSlot, LineupSlot, LineupSnapshot, PlayerRanking, DraftPick) threads `Error DBError` through.
Type signature: runDatabasePool :: (IOE :> es, Logging :> es, Error DBError :> es) => Pool -> Eff (Database : es) a -> Eff es a

runTx: the only public operation; takes a Tx.Transaction a and returns Eff es a
each call is one independent transaction; no nesting, no batching
writes commit on success; on Tx error, throwError @DBError is invoked rather than throwing IO

runDatabasePool.intent: Production interpreter: runs each runTx via Pool.runTransaction; on Left DBError, logs at ErrorS then calls throwError into the Error DBError co-effect
notes: no longer throws userError; DBError flows through the effect system
callers compose with `runErrorNoCallStack @DBError` at whatever boundary they want to handle errors
the rationale shift from throw-IO to typed-Error is captured in DbErrorAsTypedCoEffect

decisions.name: FixedTimeForTests
decisions.what: runClockFixed is the test interpreter; every now call returns the same fixed UTCTime
why: Sync code uses Clock.now to stamp synced_at on rows; tests need the same value to compare against.
An incrementing-on-each-call interpreter would test more edge cases but adds complexity.

now: the only operation; returns the current time per the active interpreter
runClockIO: IO interpreter; calls Data.Time.getCurrentTime per call
runClockFixed: fixed-time interpreter; every call returns the same UTCTime

decisions.name: TwoInterpretersHttpAndFixture
decisions.what: MLBClient has runMLBClientHTTP (production) and runMLBClientFixture (offline tests reading JSON files from disk)
why: The fixture interpreter exercises the same wire-to-domain conversion path (Pelotero.MLB.Convert) as production, just with file reads instead of HTTP.
Fixture tests don't depend on network, MLB API uptime, or rate limits.
The fixture path manually computes the SHA over teams+players bytes (same order as fetchRosters), so test-mode SHAs match production semantics.

decisions.name: FixtureBoxscoresOverride
decisions.what: MLBFixture has fixtureBoxscores :: Map Int FilePath for per-game path overrides
why: Most tests use the conventional path; the override exists for tests that need to point a specific gamePk at a corrupted/edge-case fixture file.
Avoids forcing every test to lay out its own complete fixture directory.

decisions.name: WireToDomainTeamCopiedFromFetch
decisions.what: runMLBClientFixture inlines its own copy of wireToDomainTeam rather than importing from Pelotero.MLB.Fetch
why: wireToDomainTeam is private to Fetch; exporting it for one test caller felt heavier than four lines of duplication.
If a third caller appears, this should move to a shared Convert helper.

fetchBoxscoreRaw: MLBClient send-only API for boxscore raw bytes

runMLBClientHTTP.intent: Production interpreter; delegates each operation to Pelotero.MLB.Fetch via liftIO
notes: no caching, no retries, no rate limiting at this layer

defaultFixture: constructs an MLBFixture with empty fixtureBoxscores

runMLBClientFixture.intent: Test interpreter; reads fixture files from disk and runs them through the same Convert pipeline as production

decisions.name: InMemoryFetchLogIsList
decisions.what: runFetchLogInMemory uses an IORef [FetchLogRow] (cons-prepended), not a Map
why: Tests typically write a few rows and read the most recent; a list is fine.
Cons-prepending makes 'most recent first' free.

recordFetch: FetchLog send-only; records a new fetch row
getLastFetch: FetchLog send-only; given (provider, resource, scope), returns the most recent fetch or Nothing
runFetchLogDB: requires Error DBError in the effect stack (post Phase A.3)
runFetchLogInMemory: IO-backed test interpreter using an IORef [FetchLogRow]
